chapters.title: Chapter 4: Related Parties and Capital Allocation

lessons.title: Royalty and Brand Fees Paid to Parent Companies

body.text: A royalty is paid before profit is shared. Every percentage point goes to the parent first, and reaches you only after that.

children.text: Some of the most loved stocks on NSE are Indian subsidiaries of global parents: consumer goods, auto, pharma, and industrial companies with world-famous brands and technology behind them. Many pay their parent a royalty or technical fee for using its brand, technology, or know-how. Domestic business groups do something similar through brand fees charged by the group holding company. These payments are related party transactions like any other, but they deserve their own lesson because they are large, recurring, linked to revenue rather than profit, and often rise quietly over many years.
Why Royalties Are Different From Dividends

A dividend is shared by all shareholders in proportion to their holding. A royalty is paid only to the parent, and it comes out of revenue before profit is calculated. So a parent that owns 60% of an Indian subsidiary receives 60% of the dividends plus 100% of the royalty. Every increase in the royalty rate moves profit from all shareholders to the parent alone.

body.caption: s = parent's shareholding, assuming all profit after tax is paid out as dividend

children.text: Take an illustrative subsidiary with ₹20,000 crore of revenue and ₹4,000 crore of profit before royalty and tax. The parent owns 60%, the tax rate is 25%, and all profit is paid out as dividends. Compare no royalty with a 3% royalty on revenue.

body.title: What this simplified example leaves out

children.text: Royalty received by a foreign parent is usually subject to withholding tax in India, and dividends may be taxed differently in the parent's home country, so the parent's after-tax gain is smaller than ₹330 crore. Payout ratios are also rarely 100%. None of this changes the direction of the result: a royalty shifts a share of the subsidiary's profit away from minority shareholders to the parent, and the higher the rate, the bigger the shift.

body.title: The Cost of a Royalty Hike
body.prompt: A subsidiary has revenue of ₹10,000 crore and profit after tax of ₹1,200 crore. Its parent raises the royalty rate from 1% to 4% of revenue. With a 25% tax rate, and nothing else changing, by what percentage does profit after tax fall? Answer to two decimal places.
body.explanation: Extra royalty = 3% × ₹10,000 crore = ₹300 crore. Because royalty is tax deductible, PAT falls by ₹300 crore × (1 - 0.25) = ₹225 crore. ₹225 crore ÷ ₹1,200 crore = 18.75%. Minority shareholders lose nearly a fifth of their share of profit from a change in a single contract, with no change in the business.

children.text: India removed government caps on royalty rates for foreign technology and brand agreements in 2009. After that, rates were set by the companies themselves, and several large MNC subsidiaries raised them over the following years. Concern from institutional investors led SEBI to add a specific royalty rule to the LODR Regulations in 2019.

body.label: LODR Regulation 23(1A)
body.value: Brand usage or royalty payments above 5% of annual consolidated turnover are material
body.context: Material payments need shareholder approval, and related parties, including the parent, cannot vote to approve. Below 5%, approval rests with the audit committee.

body.title: The Royalty Threshold
body.textWithBlank: Under LODR, royalty or brand usage payments to a related party become material, needing shareholder approval, when they exceed ___% of the listed company's annual consolidated turnover.
body.explanation: The 5% threshold under Regulation 23(1A) is separate from, and much lower than, the ₹1,000 crore or 10% threshold for other RPTs. Notice what it does not cover: an increase from 2% to 4.5% still needs no shareholder vote, which is why you have to track the rate yourself.

body.text: Royalty is not always a single line. Look for 'technical know-how fees', 'central services fees', 'IT and shared services', 'trademark fees', and 'cost allocation' paid to the parent or its group companies. Add them all together before comparing with the 5% threshold or with peers.

children.text: Watch the Rate, Not Just the Rupee Amount

Royalty in rupees will naturally grow with revenue. The question is whether the rate is creeping up. Consider an illustrative subsidiary whose revenue grows 8% a year from ₹10,000 crore, with an 18% operating margin before royalty and a 25% tax rate. The parent raises the royalty rate by half a percentage point every year, from 2% to 4.5%.

body.title: Royalty vs profit vs revenue (indexed, Year 1 = 100)

body.caption: The same subsidiary in rupees (₹ crore)

children.text: Revenue grew 47% over the period, but profit grew only 24%, and royalty more than tripled. By Year 6, the parent takes a royalty equal to 44% of the profit left for all shareholders, and it never needed a shareholder vote because the rate stayed below 5%. A company reporting steady revenue growth can be delivering much weaker profit growth to minority shareholders, and the royalty line explains the gap.

In 2013, Hindustan Unilever announced that its royalty and central services payments to Unilever would rise in phases from about 1.4% of turnover to 3.15% over five years. The company argued the increase reflected the value of Unilever's brands, technology, and global services. Many investors saw it as a large, permanent shift of profit to the parent that minority shareholders had no vote on. It became one of the reference cases in the debate that later led to SEBI's royalty threshold.

Domestic groups charge brand fees too. Tata Sons, the holding company of the Tata group, charges participating listed group companies a brand subscription fee linked to their revenue, with a cap linked to their profit before tax, so that a loss-making or low-margin group company does not pay a fee out of proportion to its earnings. A cap tied to profit is a useful feature to look for in any brand fee arrangement.

columns.label: Easier to Justify
points: Rate stable for many years, or linked to specific new products and technologies
Clear, disclosed list of what the subsidiary receives: patents, R&D, platforms, brand investment
Capped as a share of profit, so it falls when profits fall
Rate comparable with peer subsidiaries in the same industry
Changes put to a shareholder vote even when below the 5% threshold

columns.label: Signs of Extraction
points: Rate rising steadily with no new technology or products
Royalty growing much faster than profit
Royalty large relative to dividends paid to minority shareholders
Several separate fees to the parent that together are much larger than the headline royalty
Subsidiary also bears all local advertising and brand building costs, while paying a brand royalty

body.caption: Six numbers to track for any company paying royalty or brand fees

cells: Total royalty and similar fees ÷ revenue
Total fees ÷ dividends paid to non-parent shareholders
Royalty exceeding what minorities receive in dividends
5-year CAGR of fees vs 5-year CAGR of PAT
Fees compounding much faster than profit
Same calculation for listed peers or other subsidiaries of global companies in the sector
Public institutional votes on any royalty resolution

body.title: Which Royalty Is Most Concerning?
body.question: Four listed subsidiaries of global parents each pay a royalty. Which arrangement should concern minority shareholders the most?
options: Royalty of 3% of revenue, unchanged for ten years, with the subsidiary launching several new products based on the parent's technology
Royalty of 2% of revenue, capped at 10% of profit before tax, with the rate disclosed and explained in the annual report
Royalty that has risen from 1.5% to 4.8% of revenue over eight years, while the subsidiary's own advertising spend has also risen and profit growth has lagged revenue growth
Royalty of 4% of revenue, which shareholders approved in a vote where 88% of public institutional votes were in favour
body.explanation: Option C combines every warning sign: a rate that more than tripled, stopping just below the 5% threshold that would trigger a shareholder vote, while the subsidiary itself pays for brand building and profit growth trails revenue. The others are stable, capped, or explicitly approved by minority shareholders.

body.title: The Phased Increase
body.scenario: An Indian listed subsidiary of a European industrial group, 62% owned by the parent, announces a new technology and brand agreement. The royalty will rise from 3.0% to 4.5% of revenue in steps of 0.3 percentage points a year over five years. Because the final rate stays below 5% of consolidated turnover, no shareholder approval is needed, and the audit committee has approved it. The press release says the subsidiary will get 'access to the Group's global R&D, digital platforms, and brand portfolio'. The subsidiary's revenue is ₹8,000 crore, its PAT margin is 12%, and its tax rate is 25%. Last year it paid ₹400 crore in dividends in total.
body.prompt: Estimate the impact on minority shareholders once the full increase is in place, holding revenue constant. How should you respond as an investor?
body.modelAnswer: The increase of 1.5 percentage points on ₹8,000 crore of revenue is ₹120 crore more royalty a year. After tax at 25%, PAT falls by ₹90 crore, from ₹960 crore (12% of ₹8,000 crore) to ₹870 crore, a cut of about 9.4%. Minority shareholders own 38%, so their share of profit falls by about ₹34 crore a year, while the parent collects the full ₹120 crore of extra royalty. By the end, total royalty is ₹360 crore, close to the ₹400 crore paid as dividends to all shareholders, and about 2.4 times the roughly ₹152 crore that minorities would receive from those dividends. The rate is also set just under the 5% level that would require a vote. As an investor, ask the company to disclose exactly what new R&D, platforms, or products come with the increase, compare the rate with peer subsidiaries, write to the independent directors asking why they did not voluntarily seek shareholder approval, and adjust your valuation for lower future profit. If none of the promised benefits become visible in new products or margins, treat the royalty as a permanent governance discount.

body.title: Track the Royalty at One of Your Holdings
steps: Open the related party note in the last five annual reports and list every payment to the parent or group holding company: royalty, technical fees, brand fees, central services, IT charges
Add them up each year and divide by revenue to get the effective royalty rate
Divide total fees by profit after tax, and by dividends paid to non-promoter shareholders
Calculate the five-year CAGR of total fees and of PAT, and compare
Read the AGM notices for any royalty resolutions and check how public institutions voted
Find what the annual report says the subsidiary receives in return, and look for evidence of it in new products, margins, or market share

body.text: Companies named in this lesson are discussed based on public disclosures and widely reported announcements, for education only. The numerical examples are illustrative. Nothing here is a recommendation to buy or sell any security.

points: Royalties and brand fees go only to the parent and come out before profit is shared, so each increase shifts profit from all shareholders to the parent
In the illustration, a 3% royalty raised a 60% parent's effective share of cash to 67.6% and cut minority shareholders' dividends by 15%
LODR treats royalty or brand payments above 5% of consolidated turnover as material, needing shareholder approval without the parent voting; increases below 5% need no vote
Track the rate, not the rupee amount: add all fees to the parent, divide by revenue, and compare with PAT, minority dividends, and peers
Hindustan Unilever's 2013 phased increase from about 1.4% to 3.15% is a reference case; profit-linked caps like Tata Sons' brand fee structure are a better design
A royalty rising steadily without visible new technology or products is a governance discount that belongs in your valuation
